questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a bar is measured from zero
questions.learningObjective: explain why a bar's length must be proportional to its value
questions.stem: A bar chart shows three bars by their length, and the value axis on the left begins at 60 rather than at zero. What does the length of a bar then stand for, and what is wrong with it?

options.text: The distance from 60 up to the value, so bar length is not proportional to the value it labels
The value less 60, which is an offset every bar shares and so cancels out in any comparison
options.misconception: believes a shared offset cancels so bar lengths stay proportional

options.text: The full value, because the axis labels state the scale and a reader can add 60 back again
options.misconception: believes a labelled truncated axis keeps bar lengths honest

options.text: The value divided by 60, which normalises each bar against the lowest value on the axis
options.misconception: believes the axis minimum acts as a normalising divisor

questions.explanation: A bar is read as a length, and a length only means a quantity when it is measured from nothing, so a bar that starts at 60 measures the leftover distance and not the value. That leftover is a different number for every bar, which is exactly why a shared offset does not cancel: comparing 92 and 95 gives leftovers of 32 and 35, a ratio of about 1.09, while the values are a ratio of about 1.03. A labelled axis lets a careful reader recover each value by adding the base back, so nothing is lost, but the picture in front of the reader is a picture of the leftovers, and it is the picture that gets remembered.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader measures when the ruler is put against a bar, and where the ruler starts.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a truncated bar axis still forbids
questions.learningObjective: separate the readings a truncated axis allows from the one it breaks
questions.stem: A bar chart's value axis runs from 40 to 100, and the axis is labelled, so a reader can plainly see that it does not begin at zero. Which reading of this chart is still wrong?

options.text: Comparing one bar's length with another's, because each length starts at 40 and not at nothing
Reading the value of a single bar, because the tick labels give the number each height stands for
options.misconception: believes a labelled axis makes every kind of reading unsafe

options.text: Ranking the bars tallest to shortest, because a taller bar still means a larger value here
options.misconception: believes moving the axis base can reverse a ranking of bars

options.text: Locating 70 on the axis, because the axis carries a tick at that number and is marked
options.misconception: believes a truncated axis makes its own tick marks unreliable

questions.explanation: Truncating the base changes which readings survive and which do not, and the dividing line is whether the reading depends on a length being proportional to a value. Ranking survives because every bar gained the same 40, so the order of the lengths is untouched, and reading a single value survives because the tick labels say what each height means. A ratio of lengths does not survive: a bar of 90 is drawn 50 long and a bar of 60 is drawn 20 long, a ratio of 2.5 where the values are a ratio of 1.5. Labelling the truncation removes the deception of a hidden base, not the arithmetic error of measuring from 40.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four readings depends on a length being in proportion to a value.

questions.topic: A pie cut into too many slices
questions.learningObjective: say what a many-slice pie degrades into and what is lost
questions.stem: A pie chart is cut into eighteen slices, the smallest of which is one percent of the circle, and the reader is asked which two categories are closest in size. What does the picture become in practice?

options.text: A legend to be read against a table, because angles that close cannot be ranked by the eye
A readable part-to-whole picture, since every slice is still drawn at its true angular size
options.misconception: believes true slice sizes keep a many-slice pie readable

options.text: A picture of the largest category alone, because the eye settles on the biggest slice anyway
options.misconception: believes the eye resolves a many-slice pie down to the largest slice

options.text: A bar chart in disguise, because slice angle carries magnitude the same way a bar's length does
options.misconception: confuses judging a small angle with judging a bar on a common baseline

questions.explanation: Angle and arc length are poor channels for ranking close values, because the eye compares two positions on a common straight scale far more reliably than it compares two wedges, and the error grows as the wedge shrinks. Eighteen slices means adjacent boundaries are a few degrees apart, so asking which two are closest means asking the reader to estimate differences smaller than the picture can carry, and the honest response is to go back to the numbers. Drawing every slice correctly does not help, because the failure is in the reader's ability to discriminate, not in the drawing.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye is good at comparing, and what happens to that as the wedges shrink.

questions.topic: What a connecting segment commits to
questions.learningObjective: say what a line segment asserts about unmeasured gaps
questions.stem: A line chart joins a reading taken in March to one taken in June with a straight segment, and nothing at all was recorded in April or May. What has the drawn segment committed the chart to?

options.text: That the value moved at a steady rate in between, which is an estimate of two unmeasured months
Nothing whatsoever, because a segment is only a visual join and asserts no value between the points
options.misconception: believes a connecting segment makes no claim about the gap

options.text: That the value sat at the March reading until the June reading was finally taken
options.misconception: believes a rising segment means the value waited at its start

options.text: That April and May were measured and happened to fall along the same path
options.misconception: believes a smooth path proves the missing months were measured

questions.explanation: A straight segment has one constant slope, so drawing it commits the chart to the value having moved that way for the whole three months, and no instrument said so. The commitment is cheap when the readings are close together and expensive when they are far apart, because a real quantity usually wanders between two distant readings and can cross the drawn line several times, which the picture cannot show. A reader who trusts the line will count crossings, set a threshold on the interpolated value, and describe a shape the data never produced, so the segment is a claim that has to be defended rather than a piece of decoration.
questions.hint: Ask what a straight line with one slope says about the values between its two ends.

questions.topic: Plotting readings that have no order
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unordered axis makes a line meaningless
questions.stem: A line chart plots six measurements in whatever order the instrument happened to record them, and the result rises and falls sharply. What is the resulting line actually reporting?

options.text: A path through the readings in the order they were plotted, an order the measurements never had
A trend in the measured quantity, because a line always joins its points in time order
options.misconception: believes a connecting line always runs in time order

options.text: The spread of the readings, because the vertical extent of a line shows how variable a thing is
options.misconception: believes vertical extent of a path reports variability

options.text: A chain of causes, because the direction of travel along a line records what led to what
options.misconception: believes the order of a plotted path encodes causation

questions.explanation: A line chart carries its meaning in two places, the vertical position for the value and the horizontal position for the thing the value belongs to, and the second is what makes a rise mean an increase over something. Order the points by an instrument's switch-on times and the horizontal axis says nothing an analyst can use, so the ups and downs in the picture are a property of the recording order alone and would change if the same six readings were plotted in a different sequence. The fix is not a better-looking line but an axis that names a real ordering, and until there is one the chart should not be drawn as a line at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the horizontal position of each point stands for, and whether that thing had an order.

questions.topic: Two scales on one plot
questions.learningObjective: explain what the crossing of two dual-axis lines depends on
questions.stem: One plot carries two measures against a left axis reading 0 to 100 and a right axis reading 0 to 10, and the two lines cross in the middle of the plot area. What does that crossing establish about the measures?

options.text: Nothing about equality, because where the lines cross is fixed by the two chosen scales alone
That the two measures were equal there, because lines meet exactly where their values match
options.misconception: believes a crossing means equal values regardless of the scales

options.text: That the scales were matched, since only matched axes can put two lines in one plot
options.misconception: believes drawing two axes together proves they share a scale

options.text: That one measure drives the other, because a meeting point marks a causal link
options.misconception: believes a crossing on a dual-axis plot indicates causation

questions.explanation: With one axis the position of a point in the plot is a fact about the data, but with two axes the mapping from value to height is set twice over, and either mapping can be stretched without altering a single recorded number. Rescale the right axis to 0 to 1,000 and the same two series now cross somewhere else entirely, and the reading that they were equal at that moment was never in the data to begin with. This is why a dual-axis plot can manufacture a relationship, an intersection, or a moment where one measure overtakes another, and why the safer form is two plots that share one scale or a single plot of the difference between them.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to the crossing point if one of the two axis ranges were changed.

questions.topic: Comparing bands in a stacked area chart
questions.learningObjective: identify which band of a stack can be read off reliably
questions.stem: A stacked area chart shows three bands laid one above another, and a reader is asked how the middle band changed between two dates. What can this chart show reliably?

options.text: The bottom band alone, since it alone is measured from a flat baseline rather than a moving one
All three bands, because each band's thickness is drawn at that band's own value on one scale
options.misconception: believes every band in a stack shares one common baseline

options.text: The top edge alone, because the top edge is the sum of the three bands and so is the fixed one
options.misconception: believes only the total of a stack is a stable reading

options.text: The middle band alone, because a floating band is still measured against the band beneath it
options.misconception: believes a floating band keeps a flat reference underneath

questions.explanation: In a stack each band after the first is drawn between two curves, and the lower of those two is the sum of everything beneath it, so the band floats and its thickness has to be found by measuring between two moving lines rather than one. Measuring between two moving lines is far harder than measuring up from a floor, and the error grows with the size of the bands underneath, so the upper bands are the least readable in the chart and are usually the ones a reader most wants. The total is read reliably from the top edge, but a change in the total says nothing about which band caused it, which is the trade the stack makes.
questions.hint: Ask how many of a band's edges sit on a flat line, and how many sit on another band.

questions.topic: Bins wide enough to merge two clusters
questions.learningObjective: explain how a wide bin invents a single mode
questions.stem: A sample holds two separate clusters, one near 10 and one near 30, with nothing at all between them. Binned at a width of 50, the histogram shows one broad hump. What has the choice of bin width done to the picture?

options.text: Merged both clusters into a single bin, so the chart reports one mode the data does not contain
Dropped the smaller cluster, because a bin only keeps the values above the width it was given
options.misconception: believes a bin discards the values it cannot span

options.text: Moved the readings, because a bin recentres every value it holds on the bin's own midpoint
options.misconception: believes binning relocates the values it groups

options.text: Widened the sample, because a bin reaching further along the axis measures more of the data
options.misconception: believes a wider bin changes which values are measured

questions.explanation: A bin is a container, and a container that is wide enough to hold two separated groups will show them sitting next to each other, so the single hump is an artefact of the container rather than a property of the sample. The counts are not lost: the bin still holds every value, and moving to a narrower width splits the same total into two peaks whose heights reflect the two cluster sizes. The rule that follows is that a histogram's shape is a joint property of the data and the width chosen, so the width has to be published beside the picture and a reader who is told only that a mode exists has been told nothing about the data.
questions.hint: Ask whether a bin wide enough to span the empty middle can tell that the middle was empty.

questions.topic: Bins narrow enough to split one cluster
questions.learningObjective: explain how a narrow bin invents several modes
questions.stem: One broad cluster of readings sits evenly around 50 with no gap anywhere inside it. Binned at a width of 1, the histogram shows five peaks of equal height. What has the choice of bin width done to the picture?

options.text: Split one cluster across several bins, so the chart reports five modes the data does not contain
Found five real sub-populations, because a peak can only appear where values genuinely cluster
options.misconception: believes every peak in a histogram marks a true cluster

options.text: Rounded the readings, so values sitting near 50 drifted apart into separate small groups
options.misconception: believes binning perturbs the values it groups

options.text: Measured the sample more finely, so a narrower bin always recovers the true underlying shape
options.misconception: believes a narrower bin is always a truer measurement

questions.explanation: Narrow bins are not a free improvement, because a container narrower than the spread of a group divides that group into pieces and each piece is then reported as though it were a group of its own. Five equal peaks are what a single even cluster looks like once it is cut into five narrow containers, and the empty-looking valley between them is an artefact of the cut rather than a gap in the data. Since both the merge and the split come from the width, the width is part of the claim the chart makes and belongs in the caption, next to the count, so a reader can see how sensitive the reported shape is.
questions.hint: Ask whether the five peaks correspond to five groups in the readings or to five containers.

questions.topic: A reading sitting exactly on a bin edge
questions.learningObjective: say what decides which bin holds an edge value
questions.stem: A histogram's bins are labelled 0 to 10, 10 to 20 and 20 to 30, and one recorded reading is exactly 10. What decides which of those bars that reading is counted in?

options.text: Whether a bin takes its upper edge or not, and the label '0 to 10' leaves that unstated
Nothing decides it, because a reading on a shared edge is counted in both neighbouring bins
options.misconception: believes an edge value is counted twice in adjacent bins

options.text: Whichever bin's midpoint is nearest, because bins are compared by their centres
options.misconception: believes a value is assigned to the bin whose centre is closest

options.text: The last bin on the axis, because an edge reading is always pushed to the far end
options.misconception: believes edge values are reassigned to the final bin

questions.explanation: Two bins share every edge, so a value sitting exactly on one has to be given to one side or the other, and the choice is made by a rule rather than by the data. Bins written as half-open intervals, with the lower edge included and the upper excluded, make every value land in exactly one bin, and the opposite convention does the same with the edges reversed; what changes between them is only which bar a boundary value is counted in. That sounds cosmetic until the values cluster on round numbers, which measured quantities very often do, and then the two conventions produce visibly different bar heights for identical data.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two bars sharing that edge takes the value, and where that rule is written down.

questions.topic: A smoothed curve between observations
questions.learningObjective: explain what a fitted curve adds to a sparse series
questions.stem: A line chart of twelve monthly readings is drawn as a smooth curve that rises, dips and turns between the markers. What has been put into the picture that no instrument measured?

options.text: Values in the gaps between readings, invented by the curve's shape and finer than the data
Nothing at all, because a smooth curve through the same markers is the same data drawn neatly
options.misconception: believes smoothing adds no information to a series

options.text: Extra readings, because each turning point of the curve is another measurement of the series
options.misconception: believes a fitted curve reports additional measurements

options.text: A measured trend, because any curve passing through every marker exposes the underlying trend
options.misconception: believes a curve through the points reports a measured trend

questions.explanation: Fitting a curve is choosing a rule for the gaps, and the rule writes in as many values as there are positions between the markers, each with a false precision that the raw readings do not have. The turning points are the worst of it, because they are where the curve's own shape rather than any measurement decides the value, so a reader can end up describing a feature of the fitting method as a feature of the world. Smoothing is defensible as a way of seeing the coarse shape, and indefensible as a way of reporting detail, which is why the markers belong on the same picture as the curve whenever the curve is published.
questions.hint: Ask how many values the curve draws between two markers, and where they came from.

questions.topic: A filled area drawn between daily counts
questions.learningObjective: explain what a continuous fill claims about discrete counts
questions.stem: A filled area chart plots the number of tickets closed on each of ten separate days, and the shading runs without a break from one day to the next. What does that unbroken shading claim that the counts cannot support?

options.text: That a part-closed ticket existed on the days in between, a quantity nobody ever counted
Nothing at all, since the shading only fills in under points that were genuinely recorded
options.misconception: believes a filled area adds no values between its points

options.text: That the daily counts were rising, because a filled shape has to slope upward to look full
options.misconception: believes a filled area is only used for rising series

options.text: That the days were of equal length, because a continuous fill can only span equal intervals
options.misconception: believes a filled area requires evenly spaced observations

questions.explanation: Shading under a line is a claim that the quantity exists everywhere along the axis, not only at the marked points, and that claim is true for a quantity that genuinely varies continuously and false for one that is tallied at intervals. A count of tickets closed on a day is a tally of whole events on that day, and a smooth shaded ramp between two tallies implies fractional tickets on the days in between, which is not a thing the counting process can produce. Where the quantity really is continuous, the fill is exactly the right form; where it is a tally, the honest form is a bar per interval, because a bar's own width carries the fact that the value belongs to a whole period.
questions.hint: Ask whether a fraction of a ticket closed on a day between two tallies is a real quantity.

questions.topic: Reading the spacing on a log axis
questions.learningObjective: explain why equal spacing on a log axis is read wrongly as linear
questions.stem: A value axis is logarithmic and runs from 10 to 10,000, so equal distances along it stand for equal multiplications. A reader studies the spacing and concludes that growth has stalled. Where has that reader gone wrong?

options.text: Equal spacing was read as equal addition, but 10 to 20 is as wide as 5,000 to 10,000
The axis must be broken, because no log scale can span three decades of value
options.misconception: believes a log scale cannot cover a wide range of values

options.text: The axis was read from the wrong end, because log scales count down from the largest value
options.misconception: believes a log axis runs from large values down to small ones

options.text: The readings must be wrong, because no rising series can flatten on any axis at all
options.misconception: believes a rising series cannot look flat on a log axis

Reading the spacing as though the same room stood for the same addition is the mistake, and it is a natural one because linear axes are far more common. The scale is the right choice when the values span orders of magnitude and the quantity of interest is proportional change, and the label has to say in words that the steps are multiplications, because the tick numbers alone do not tell a hurried reader which kind of axis is in front of them.
questions.hint: Ask how wide the step from 10 to 20 is compared with the step from 5,000 to 10,000.

questions.topic: Shading a map by raw counts
questions.learningObjective: explain what a count-shaded map reports instead of risk
questions.stem: A map shades every region by its raw count of reported events, and the region with the largest population is also the darkest. What does a reader take from the shading?

options.text: That the largest region carries the highest risk, when it may simply have the most people reporting
That risk is spread evenly, because every region is given a shade from one shared scale
options.misconception: believes a single colour scale implies the risk is evenly spread

options.text: That the smallest region is safest, because a low count is always also a low rate
options.misconception: believes a small count proves a small rate

options.text: That the map measures population, because a count and a population shade the same way
options.misconception: believes a count-shaded map reports population density

Shading by rate fixes the comparison between regions of different sizes, and when raw counts matter too the two belong in two pictures or in one picture with the count printed on the region.

A zero point, because a colour scale has to begin at nothing the way a bar axis does

Nothing at all, because a value read off a plotted point is the recorded number itself
options.misconception: believes a value read off a plot is exact

options.text: The width of the chart alone, because a wide plot is the only thing that blurs a reading
options.misconception: believes plot width is the only source of read-off error

The line is unbroken, so a shortened axis cannot distort a shape drawn along it at all
options.misconception: believes a continuous line is immune to a shortened axis

options.text: The axis is vertical, since only distances along a horizontal axis are read proportionally
options.misconception: believes only horizontal distances are read proportionally

options.text: The readings sit close together, so any axis holding them shows the same shape anyway

The condition for the shortened axis to be honest is that the reader can see the whole range, which is why the labelled ticks are what make it defensible rather than the choice of base itself.

questions.learningObjective: read a categorical line chart as an artefact of its order
questions.stem: A line chart plots each month's total in alphabetical order: April, August, December, February, January, July, June, March, May, November, October, September. The line rises, falls and rises again across the page. What is that shape made of?

options.text: A path through months sorted by name, so every rise and fall belongs to the alphabet alone
The year's pattern, since a line chart always reads left to right in time order
options.misconception: believes a line chart always runs in time order

options.text: A seasonal effect, because months near each other in the year sit near each other here
options.misconception: believes alphabetical order preserves the year's sequence

options.text: A falling year, since a line ending lower than it began always reports a decline
options.misconception: believes the final height alone reports a trend

questions.explanation: Sorting twelve months by name puts December third and January fifth, so the line leaps between points that are six months apart in the year and then draws a long flat run across two names that are one month apart. Every turning point in the picture is therefore a property of the alphabet and would move if the months were listed in any other order, including the order that would make the year look like it fell. The values themselves are untouched, which is what makes this so easy to miss: the chart is not wrong about any number, only about what the horizontal direction means, so the fix is to order the axis by the thing being measured.

questions.topic: Why bars and lines answer to different baselines
questions.learningObjective: explain the encoding that makes a raised baseline a fault on bars only
questions.stem: A bar chart's value axis begins at 60 and a line chart's value axis begins at 88. Explain why the same choice of starting point is treated as a fault on one form and as a decision on the other.

answer.exemplar: The difference comes from what the reader measures. A bar's length has nothing to be compared against except the other bars and the empty space below it, so a bar that starts at 60 measures the leftover distance and every bar carries a different one; the chart therefore reports 4 where the data says 1.5, and no label repairs that, because the label describes the axis while the length describes the bar. A line's height, on the other hand, is read against the axis, and the axis states in words what each height means, so moving the base changes how steep the movement looks without changing which reading was higher. That is why the rule is a base of zero for bars and a labelled base for lines, and why a line at 88 is only honest when the reader can see 88, 90 and 100 rather than a bare truncated stub: the condition is not the base but the visibility of the whole range.

questions.explanation: An answer has to name the two encodings rather than the two forms, because a bar encodes magnitude as length measured from an implied nothing while a line encodes it as position read against a stated scale. Without that, the explanation is a rule of thumb with no reason attached, and a reader who disagrees with the rule has nothing to weigh.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader measures when the ruler goes against a bar, and against a line.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a histogram's shape depends on its bin width
questions.stem: The same 200 response times are charted three times, and the three histograms show one broad hump, two humps and four humps as the bin width is reduced. Explain what is happening, and state what a published histogram must say about itself.

answer.exemplar: The values are fixed and only the container is changing, so every difference in shape is produced by the binning. A width of 20 seconds is coarse enough to hold two separated groups at once, so the gap between them is swallowed and the picture reports one mode the sample does not have. A width of 4 seconds is narrow enough to cut a single broad group into several, so the picture now reports four modes the sample does not have, and the valleys between them are artefacts of the cut rather than gaps in the data. Nothing is discovered at either width; the same 200 values are in all three charts, and the honest statement is that the shape is a joint property of the data and the width. So a published histogram has to carry the width in its caption, has to carry the bin edges, has to say how values falling on an edge were assigned, and has to say the sample size, because without those four things a reader cannot tell which features of the shape are in the data. Where the shape changes as the width changes, the report should show more than one width or say plainly that it is sensitive to the choice, rather than publishing the version that reads best.

questions.explanation: An answer that says only that the bins are too coarse or too fine has not answered the question, because it leaves the reader unsure whether one of the three charts is true. The mechanism is that the data is identical in all three and the container is not, which makes the width a claim rather than a formatting detail.

answer.exemplar: The three figures answer three different questions. The median of 1 minute answers what a typical caller experienced, because half the calls waited less and half waited more, so the long tail cannot move it at all. The mean of 6 minutes answers what the total waiting time divided by the number of calls comes to, which is the right number for costing a team of agents and the wrong number for describing an experience, because a small number of very long calls lift it sixfold without changing what most callers went through. The longest wait of 3 hours answers the question a median cannot, which is how bad the worst case gets, and that is the figure that determines whether a queue is safe to leave unattended overnight. So the top of an operations report belongs to the median, with the mean beside it for costing and the worst case beside that for risk, and a report that leads with the mean alone will staff for a queue that most callers never enter while under-staffing the one they do. The honest arrangement publishes all three and states which question each answers, rather than choosing one and letting the reader assume it is the answer to the others.

questions.explanation: An answer that picks the median and calls the mean wrong has chosen correctly but not taught, because the reader still does not know which figure to use for staffing or for costing. Naming the question each figure answers is the part that makes the choice usable.

questions.topic: A tracking claim resting on two chosen scales
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a dual-axis claim and say what would support it
questions.stem: Two measures are drawn against a left axis running 0 to 100 and a right axis running 0 to 10, and the caption claims the two track each other. Explain how far that conclusion depends on the two scales, and say what would have to be shown to support the claim.

answer.exemplar: The conclusion depends on the scales entirely, because with two axes the height of a point is set twice over and either mapping can be stretched without altering a single recorded value. Rescale the right axis to 0 to 1,000 and lines that were rising together now flatten, and rescale it to 0 to 1 and the same two series now appear to cross twice, so an intersection, a lead and a moment of overtaking are all artefacts of two choices the reader cannot see. That is why a dual-axis plot can manufacture a relationship out of unrelated series and why the caption's claim is not merely weakly supported but unfalsifiable from the picture: there is no view of this plot that would refute it. To support a tracking claim, a report has to show that the relationship survives the rescaling, which means plotting both measures against one shared scale, or plotting the difference or the ratio of the two against a single axis and showing that it stays inside a stated band, or showing the two in separate stacked panels that share a horizontal scale. The first says whether they move together in absolute terms, the second and third say whether they move together in relative terms, and a caption has to say which of the three it means. A caption that says they track each other while the plot lets either scale be chosen freely has claimed the one thing the plot is built not to show.

questions.explanation: An answer has to make the dependence concrete, because saying only that two scales can be misleading leaves the reader unable to tell whether this particular pair is misleading. Rescaling one axis and watching the relationship change is what turns the point into a test.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the claimed relationship if one of the two axis ranges is changed.

A caption adds words to correct a picture that is still wrong, since the reader who glances will not read it and the reader who does read it already suspected the problem. A shorter window is the same fault with a smaller number, and a second axis does not let anybody check the first, it just gives a second thing to misread.

questions.topic: Requirements for a map a reader can act on
questions.learningObjective: select a shading measure that satisfies two stated map requirements
questions.stem: A team must show regional risk on a map where the requirements are that every district is shaded by something comparable between districts and that a reader can turn any shade back into a number. Which measure meets both requirements?

options.text: Shade by rate per 100,000 and label the legend from the lowest to the highest rate with a number at each end
Shade by total cases and print each district's population in the middle of its shape
options.misconception: believes printing a population beside a count shades the map by rate

options.text: Shade by total cases and use a second darker shade wherever a district passes a fixed count
options.misconception: believes a second shade makes counts comparable across districts

options.text: Shade by rate and place a bar chart of the raw counts in a panel beside the map
options.misconception: believes a separate panel lets a shade be read as a number

questions.explanation: The two requirements are about different jobs and each one eliminates a different family of options, so an answer has to satisfy both rather than sound good on one. Only the rate is comparable between districts of different sizes, which rules out every option built on raw counts, and only a legend with labelled endpoints turns a shade into a number, which rules out the arrangement that puts the counts in a separate panel where a reader holding the map has to look somewhere else. The count information is not lost by shading the rate, it is moved to the panel or the district label where it belongs, since the workload and the risk are two different facts and a single map can only carry one of them as a shade.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Plotting a day the collector never recorded
questions.learningObjective: choose how a gap is shown so it is not read as a measurement
questions.stem: A daily series is missing one day because the collector was offline, and the team must plot it so the gap is not read as a fall to zero while still showing the days either side of it. Which measure does that?

options.text: Leave the day blank so the line breaks, and note the day and the reason it is empty
Carry the previous day's value across the gap, so the line stays unbroken and nothing looks wrong
options.misconception: believes carrying a value forward records what happened

options.text: Plot the day at zero, so the size of the hole is visible in the shape of the line
options.misconception: believes a zero is the clearest way to mark an absence

options.text: Fit a smooth curve through the days either side, so the missing value can be read from the fit
options.misconception: believes a fitted value can stand in for a recorded one

questions.explanation: The requirement is that the gap must not be mistaken for a value, and only a blank achieves that, because a break in the line is visibly something other than a reading while each of the other three fills the hole with a number the collector never produced. Carrying the previous value forward states that the quantity held steady, plotting a zero states that it fell to nothing, and a fitted curve states that it moved along the path the fit chose, so all three convert an absence into a claim and each one is wrong whenever the reason for the outage is the interesting part. Leaving it blank and saying why costs one note and keeps the fact that the run was broken visible, which is usually the fact a reader most needs.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four fills the hole with a number, and whether the collector ever reported one.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Showing twelve monthly readings without inventing the rest
questions.learningObjective: select a form that shows discrete observations and nothing between them
questions.stem: A report must show a metric measured once at the end of each of twelve months, where the requirements are that every measured figure stays visible and that no value between two months is presented as a measured one. Which form is safest?

options.text: Draw one bar per month from a zero baseline and print each measured figure on it
Plot the twelve measured points and join consecutive ones with straight segments, as any line does
options.misconception: believes a connecting segment presents no value in between

options.text: Plot a smooth curve fitted through the twelve points, so the month-to-month shape reads easily
options.misconception: believes a fitted curve reports a measured shape between months

options.text: Fill the area from the baseline up to each monthly value, so the year reads as one total
options.misconception: believes a filled area avoids implying values between readings

questions.explanation: Each of the twelve figures is a tally taken at one moment, so the form has to keep each value attached to its own month and draw nothing in the spaces between, and one bar per month does both while its own width states that the value belongs to a whole period. A straight segment is the mild version of the same problem, since it asserts a steady rate across a month that was only sampled once, and it is easy to forget because it is the convention almost every line chart follows. A fitted curve and a filled area both go further, inventing a turning point and a continuum that no measurement supports, and the reason they look good is the reason they are dangerous: they are easier to read than the truth.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four forms draws anything in the space between two months.
